newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Consumers to propel British growth in 97.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Consumers to propel British growth in 97.

text.p: British growth could see a bumper year, with consumer spending propelling gross domestic product (GDP) to 3.6 percent by the third quarter of 1997, Reuters quarterly poll of economic forecasts published on Monday showed.
But after good times in 1997, GDP could find itself a little hungover in 1998 under a new government which may raise interest rates and taxes.
Many consumers are set to rake in the cash from bonus payments on savings accounts giving them a higher disposable income which could swell high street sales, economists said.

"You've got building society windfalls, recent tax cuts from the last budget, maturing TESSAs (tax-exempt special savings accounts) and stronger house prices, so all of these should feed through," said Howard Archer, research manager at Natwest Group.

The average of predictions for GDP showed growth reaching 2.8 percent in the final quarter of 1996 before peaking at 3.6 percent in the third quarter of 1997. The average forecast for 1997 as a whole was 3.4 percent with individual numbers ranging from 2.8 to 4.3 percent.

Latest figures released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) showed GDP at 2.2 percent in the third quarter of 1996. Reuters poll was conducted between January 6 and 8 and 40 economists provided GDP forecasts.

A general election must be held by May 22, and while opposition Labour are widely expected to oust the ruling Conservatives, economists said purse strings would have to be tightened next year, whichever party came to power.

"You'll have a combination of tighter fiscal policy, tighter monetary policy and a cyclical slowdown. Unemployment will bottom out and you'll have the end of the spending effects of the windfalls...and hence growth will slow at the end of 1998," said Andrew Snowball, Treasury Economist at Co-operative Bank.
The poll predicted GDP will taper off to 2.5 percent by the third quarter of 1998.

Forecasts for industrial production followed the same pattern, averaging 1.5 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 before rising to a peak of 3.7 percent in the third quarter of 1997. By the following year it would slow to 2.2 percent, the poll predicted. The November figure of 1.3 percent was released after the poll closed.
But while some predicted strong GDP growth in 1997, other economists saw subdued conditions in Europe putting a lid on growth in Britain.
"Generally in Europe we're not seeing a strong acceleration and therefore you're not going to see much of an impact in the UK from exports," said Sharda Persaud, European economist at San Paolo Bank.
And it is difficult to predict how much of the windfall cash will find its way to the high street.

"We've seen a big increase in things like personal equity plans and so windfalls are probably most likely to be saved in this current climate," said Persaud. "You are seeing a pick-up in the housing market which will help but I dont think that is going to filter down too much to durable goods and the retail sector."
December's distributive trades survey from the Confederation of British Industry, released on January 10 after the poll closed, showed healthy retail sales, but growth was well below expectations.
